idiom_name: state in the narrowest-lived owner: block-scope locals and a caller-owned struct; file-scope static only for genuinely module-private state
implementation_notes: C has no components, so state colocation becomes scope discipline. Declare each value in the innermost block that uses it - block-scope objects have automatic storage duration and die when the block exits - and give a widget, screen or subsystem its own struct instance, passed by pointer to the functions that operate on it, so the state lives exactly as long as its owner. The replacement for the classic structure is therefore the caller-owned struct: instead of one shared state record that the whole UI reads and writes (the C equivalent of an app-level store), each owner carries its struct and only genuinely shared values get a common owner. File-scope static variables (internal linkage) and thread-local state are the program-lifetime exception and are justified only when one translation unit really owns a single instance; document who owns the shared struct when several widgets must observe one value, because nothing in the language will.
pitfalls: A file-scope static (or a global) has static storage duration and lives for the whole program; reaching for it is the C way of hoisting state to the application root, so reserve it for one-instance module state and name the owner in a comment.
Storing a pointer to a caller-owned struct outlives the caller's frame if the pointer is kept; every callback context must be documented with the lifetime of the struct it points to, or it dangles.

Whether a widget gets its own struct instance or shares one must be decided explicitly: sharing a mutable struct across screens or threads without an owner and a lock turns colocated state into a data race.
